content: Neonatal prophylaxis may be considered as a viable option. In the absence of maternal antiretroviral therapy, a standard infant prophylaxis regimen consisting of six weeks of zidovudine has been shown to effectively reduce the risk of HIV transmission compared to no prophylaxis, as evidenced by epidemiologic data from resource-rich countries. A South African study involving infants born to mothers who did not receive antenatal or intrapartum antiretroviral (ARV) drug regimens found no significant difference in overall perinatal transmission rates between infants who received a single dose of nevirapine within 24 hours of delivery and those who underwent six weeks of zidovudine therapy. However, a trial conducted in Malawi with breastfeeding infants demonstrated that adding one week of zidovudine therapy to a single dose of infant nevirapine reduced the risk of HIV transmission by 36% compared to using infant nevirapine alone. To determine the optimal infant prophylaxis regimen in formula-fed populations where maternal antepartum ARV drug administration is absent, the NICHD-HPTN 040/P1043 multicountry clinical trial (conducted in Argentina, Brazil, South Africa, and the United States) enrolled 1,735 formula-fed infants born to HIV-infected mothers who had not received ARV drugs during the current pregnancy prior to labor. If women presented early enough, intravenous intrapartum zidovudine was administered. The study compared three infant ARV regimens: (1) six weeks of zidovudine alone, (2) six weeks of zidovudine plus three doses of nevirapine administered during the first week of life (at birth to 48 hours, 48 hours after the first dose, and 96 hours after the second dose), and (3) six weeks of zidovudine combined with lamivudine and nelfinavir given from birth through two weeks of age. The findings, presented at the 2011 Conference on Retroviruses and Opportunistic Infections, revealed that combination regimens reduced the risk of intrapartum HIV transmission by approximately 50% compared to zidovudine monotherapy. Based on these results, combination ARV prophylaxis is now recommended in the United States for infants whose mothers did not receive antenatal ARV drugs. Several studies conducted in formula-fed and breastfed populations in resource-limited settings have shown that adding maternal or infant single-dose nevirapine to a maternal short-course zidovudine or zidovudine/lamivudine regimen enhances efficacy compared to the short-course regimen alone. However, the efficacy of single-dose nevirapine when combined with the standard recommended combination ARV prophylaxis regimens used in the United States was evaluated in the PACTG 316 clinical trial, conducted in the United States, Europe, Brazil, and the Bahamas. This study demonstrated that for non-breastfeeding women in resource-rich countries, the addition of single-dose nevirapine did not provide significant benefit in the context of combination ARV prophylaxis throughout pregnancy and very low viral loads at delivery. Consequently, the use of single-dose intrapartum nevirapine is generally not recommended for women in the United States who are receiving standard antenatal ARV prophylaxis. Breastfeeding by HIV-infected women, including those receiving ARV drugs, is not recommended in the United States where replacement feeding is affordable, feasible, acceptable, sustainable, and safe, and where the risk of infant mortality due to diarrheal and respiratory infections is low. Numerous studies have evaluated the use of maternal or infant ARV prophylaxis during breastfeeding to reduce postnatal HIV transmission. Observational data and randomized clinical trials have demonstrated that infant prophylaxis, primarily using daily infant nevirapine during breastfeeding, significantly reduces the risk of postnatal HIV transmission through breast milk. Similarly, maternal triple-drug prophylaxis during breastfeeding has been shown to decrease postnatal HIV infection rates.
